stories.title: The psychology of kicking or recieving
stories.summary:
The Bills accepted the ball last week against the Lions after winning the coin toss and marched down the field and scored a TD.  Maybe it was just to have a Bill be the first to score in the new Highmark, but with this juggernaut offense and a weak defense, there may be more to it than that.



	 



	Opposing teams know when they play the Bills they are probably walking into a shoot out.  Some hope they can keep up, others hope to slow the game so much that it keeps #17 on the bench and not on the field scoring touchdowns.  



	 



	I think there is something to be said for the Bills takeing the ball first.  If the Bills score on the opening drive, it immediately puts pressure on the other team to keep up.  Putting the Bills' offense out there also puts the Bills' best foot forward.  The offense is a lot more likely to score than the Bills' defense is to stop the other offense from scoring. 



	 



	If the opposing team recieves the ball and marches down the field and scores, it gives them a boost of confidence that they can hang.  On the other hand, if they watch #17 carve them up on the opening drive like he did on Thursday night, it sets the tone and they have to feel like they are going to be in for a long game.



	 



	I like accepting the ball and making the opening drive.  I think it plays to the Bills' strengths and effects the psychology of the game.  I hope they do it again this week agaisnt the Bolts.

stories.title: The Bills "Core Four", and the similarities to the Super Bowl Era Chiefs "Core Four"...
stories.summary:
When the Chiefs were at their most dominant, their 4 best players were Mahomes, Tyreek Hill, Travis Kelce, and Chris Jones.



	 



	The Bills current 4 best players right now play the exact same 4 positions....Josh Allen, DJ Moore, Dalton Kincaid, and Deone Walker.



	 



	Can the Bills "Core Four" lead this team in the next few years to the same success of those Chiefs teams??



	 



	I don't know the answer, but I think we are going to have a lot of fun watching it all unfold!!



	 



	Go Bills!!!!

stories.title: Deep pass still not there
stories.summary:
Granted, the offense has looked excellent the first two weeks, but the one thing that still hasn't improved is Allen's accuracy on the deep ball. He's pretty much been consistently excellent at everything the past few years except that one area. I know part of it is not having the weapons at receiver to accomplish this, but even when he has, he hasn't been great at it.



	 



	The pass to Shakir this past Thursday and the underthrow to Moore the week before (resulted in a DPI, luckily) are just the latest examples of inaccurate throws where Allen lets it rip but doesn't drop it where it needs to be. Even the TD to Palmer on that busted coverage against the Lions was underthrown.



	 



	He's hit on his share as well, not saying he's completely inept at it. But there is a lot of room for improvement. At this point, I'm not sure if that's ever going to be a consistent weapon in his arsenal. If he ever does get that part of his game sorted however, this offense will truly be unstoppable.

Replay assist should be changed or abolished
stories.summary:
I get why they wanted to do replay assist. But there is no way to apply it in a fair and non-arbitrary manner. Last night, the Colts had to use a regular replay challenge on a spot, and risk losing a TO. Why wasn’t replay assist used instead? No one knows. 
	 



	my proposal would be: 



	 



	1) abolish replay assist; or 



	 



	2) use it automatically for certain defined things on the request of any coach (eg, for every 3rd or 4th down spot that is questioned by a team).

stories.summary:
Quick Hits as We Prepare to Kick Off the Season



We are getting close, Sabres fans. Off the heels of their first playoff appearance in forever, the 2026-27 season is inching closer.



Many NHL pundits, YouTubers and NHL fans are expecting a drop-off from Buffalo. I do too—to an extent. I doubt the Sabres reach 109 points again, but I still expect them to be a good, competitive team and probably finish second or third in the Atlantic Division.



Look around elsewhere, though, and you will see some much more pessimistic predictions. Fourth place seems to be the common expectation, with some projections dropping Buffalo all the way to seventh. The losses of Alex Tuch and Bowen Byram certainly factor into that, but I think there is also a widespread belief that last season was simply a one-year fluke.



Well, let’s see what the Blue and Gold have in store for us. Hockey is almost upon us again.



As the season approaches, here are a few quick hits on my mind as we get ready for another year of Buffalo Sabres hockey.




GOALTENDING: Ukko-Pekka Luukkonen and Alex Lyon gave Buffalo a pretty reliable tandem last season in net, and having Colton Ellis developing right behind them gives the organization some additional depth. There were some breakdowns in the playoffs from both goalies for sure but I fully expect a return to form. Luukkonen in particular seems to be in a good mindset. And compared with some of the other question marks on the roster, I wouldn’t be surprised if goaltending ends up being viewed as a strength again. Many forget that the Buffalo Sabres team save percentage last year was .907 (ranking third in the NHL)



TEAM TOUGHNESS: The losses of Jordan Greenway, Josh Dunne and even Logan Stanley leave the Sabres noticeably short on toughness. Louis Crevier adds some much-needed size and physicality, but I’m not sure it’s enough. Especially among the forward ranks. That could make games against the Florida Panthers and Tampa Bay Lightning especially challenging this season. The Sabres win with speed and scoring but some teams will try to drag Buffalo down with cheap shots and punishing play. I’m not sure they have the horses to handle that.



BORDERS: We all know the Sabres sing both anthems at every home game because of their proximity to Canada and large Southern Ontario fan base. All seven Canadian teams do the same, regardless of the opponent. Not to get political, (you either, please!) but that could make for some interesting times this season if Canada’s political ire with the United States starts to show at games. We love and support our Northern neighbors in general and sure hope our Southern Ontario fans stick with the team!











TAZ TIME: Fresh off The Athletic’s 2026 U23 rankings — and Corey Pronman’s rather baffling 124th-overall placement of Zach Benson — our lovable carnie looks ready to further cement his legend. Benson now has his new seven-year deal, three NHL seasons under his belt and a memorable playoff run behind him. Now, he’s ready to take the next step offensively. I believe Taz is going to break out with 20-plus goals and 60-plus points this season. The offensive numbers should take a significant jump, but the hard-working, tenacious pest of a player isn’t going anywhere. That relentless style is a huge part of what makes Benson so effective, regardless of how much offense he produces. Zach is already a young cornerstone for this franchise, and after what he showed in the playoffs, I’m expecting him to take another big step forward in 2026-27.



NO CHANGES: The Buffalo Sabres signed head coach Lindy Ruff to a two-year contract extension back in May and retained his entire coaching staff. After the amazing success this team had last season, that decision wasn’t particularly surprising. But two problem areas remain that this same coaching staff has yet to figure out—and they will have another season to try. The power-play and face-offs. Buffalo’s man advantage was dreadful for long stretches last season. Inept, lost and seemingly helpless at times, the Sabres finished 20th in the NHL at 19.5%. That’s not an outright disaster on paper, but there were far too many stretches where the power play looked completely out of sync. Then there’s the face-off issue, which has been an Achilles’ heel for the Sabres for quite some time. They bottomed out last season, finishing 32nd in the NHL at just 45.9%. That’s not a minor weakness—it’s a problem that can consistently put a team behind the eight ball. Maybe Buffalo simply learns to work around these deficiencies again. Maybe the power-play improves with better execution and another year of familiarity. Maybe the face-off numbers bounce back naturally. To me, these are still two glaring weaknesses. They could eventually drag this team down or force Buffalo to continue finding ways to win despite them. EDIT: Most of these topics were written one to two weeks ago before I was out of town for 10 days. Since then, the Sabres have expanded the role of assistant to the GM Eric Staal, who will now assist with Buffalo’s power play. Lindy Ruff has some ideas and wants to instill Staal’s success as a player on the man advantage into the Sabres’ system. Ruff desires to “Get the power play lower on the ice and not above the circle, getting below the hash marks, and getting more people closer to the net.” In his career, Staal scored 133 power-play goals, including six straight seasons with 12 or more on the man advantage. Lindy’s new approach while adding Eric’s successful experience shows the team knows they have to be better, and that is an encouraging sign.



DOANER: Josh Doan left a strong first-year impression in Buffalo, scoring 25 goals and 52 points. For the Sabres to make the playoffs again, they’ll need another strong season from No. 91. Scratch that—they’ll need an even better one. Doan is expected to see more time in the top-six this season, so scoring 30 goals and 65 points is a very realistic target. He also showed he can elevate his game when it matters most, scoring three goals and 10 points in 13 playoff games during his first trip to the Stanley Cup Playoffs. He was one of Buffalo’s better players throughout the postseason. I fully expect Doan to pick up right where he left off when October rolls around. If he takes that next step offensively, it could be a huge boost for the Sabres.









ZELLY: I have said this elsewhere, but I really feel like Olen Zellweger can be Bo Byram-Lite this season. He has many of the same attributes, including being a sound shooter and skilled puck distributor. Olen also has great speed and plays the 200-foot game Lindy Ruff wants from his defensemen. He just turned 23 and only has parts of three NHL seasons under his belt, so Bo still has the advantage when it comes to experience and development at the NHL level. Byram also refined his defensive game with the Sabres this past year before bolting for the big bucks, and Zellweger still needs to do the same. Offensively, though, he has a lot to offer and possesses a similar skill set. He scored seven goals and 22 points with the Ducks last season. In Buffalo’s system, I believe he can elevate those numbers and potentially approach Bo-like production. If he gets mostly 2nd pairing duty, I expect Olen to put up 35-to-40-points for the Sabres, and honestly, I’d be surprised if he didn’t.



DBTB: Lastly, with another Buffalo Sabres hockey season upon us, I’d like to take a moment and thank all the fellow knuckleheads here on the site. We have gone though hell and back for 14 seasons and were finally rewarded with good fortune in 2025-26. It was quite a run by our boys and more good things are expected of them. So here is to another playoff bound season (we all hope) and more good fortune than you can shake a Beer Sabre at! After this season, I want to see a hundred memes of sad faced Bo and Alex looking up at the Sabres skating around with the Cup. Make that happen, please.

Buffalo Sabres Top 25 Under 25: #1 Zach Benson
stories.summary:
The Top 25 Under 25 is a collaboration by members of the Die By The Blade community. 92 readers ranked Buffalo Sabres players under the age of 25 as of August 1, 2026. Each participant used their own metric of current ability and production to rank each player.



Zach Benson



Drafted: 2023, BUF (13th overall), 1st round, 13th pick



Position: Left Wing



Born: 5/12/2005 (Age: 21) Chilliwack, British Columbia, CAN



2025-2026 stats: GP 65 G 13 A 30 PTS 43 +27, Buffalo Sabres



2025 T25U25 Ranking: 2nd last year



I had Zach Benson last year when he was ranked #2 and I get him again at #1 in the 2026 rankings. What I said about him last season still holds true.




“Benson brings high energy to the rink and is stong on the forecheck, even at his limited size. (5’10” and 177 pounds now UPDATED) He is a physical sparkplug out there, not afraid of contact. He does take some bad penalties sometimes, which he needs to work on. But he also takes some highly questionable phantom calls as well. Frequently, it really feels like the referees are targeting this little fella of ours. He just wants to be an UNDERSIZED TERROR, let him play his game!



Zach also has the heart of a lion and a good motor on him. He can be chirpy out there too and is always in on any scrum that develops.”









Benson did cut down on the penalties last season, while his offense took a major step forward. Benny popped off for 13 goals and 30 assists, totaling 43 points in just 65 games—all career highs.



Taz also registered five goals and nine points in 13 playoff games, where fans outside of Buffalo really began to take notice. It wasn’t just the points he piled up, either. His relentless forechecking, non-stop motor, and incredible work ethic were on full display.










Benson really elevated his reputation during the 2026 Stanley Cup Playoffs, despite what some fool who works at The Athletic had to say a few weeks back. He has elite vision and puck distribution all while earning praise as a “bulldog” for his high-energy style of play, physical board battles, and clutch scoring.



Taz is a wonderful pest to have on our team and he is one of the better two-way young forwards in the NHL. I believe he can light the lamp even more going forward and I think a 60 point season is in the cards for Mr. Benson this year. He will get plenty of playing time in the top-six.







Taz Fun Fact: Benson ranked second in the NHL behind Connor McDavid (10.57) in miles skated per 60 on the penalty kill (10.25).

stories.title: The time is now
stories.summary:
The Sabres’ window to win is wide open. They can’t afford to waste it again.



The Sabres need to stop treating their best chance to win as something always a few years away. With Tage Thompson and Rasmus Dahlin under contract, the foundation is already here. Buffalo should be building a team capable of competing for a Stanley Cup while those deals are in place. Every season spent waiting for the perfect roster is another season lost.



Thompson carries a cap hit of roughly $7.14 million through 2029–30, while Dahlin is signed at $11 million annually through 2031–32. That gives Buffalo four more seasons with both players on their current contracts. Four seasons can sound like plenty of time, until one becomes another development year and the next becomes another year spent fixing the same problems. The Sabres need to approach that stretch with a clear expectation of winning. Thompson contract details⁠, Dahlin contract details⁠, via PuckPedia



Thompson’s deal is especially valuable because it lets Buffalo build around him. Getting that kind of goal scoring for just over $7 million should leave room to build a deeper, more complete team. Dahlin’s contract is a larger investment, but it gives the organization certainty at one of the hardest positions to fill. With the contracts being handed out this summer, fans can thank the COVID-era static cap growth. Buffalo knows the cost of two foundational players for years. Management should be using this certainty to address weaknesses and give them a legitimate chance to win.



Alex Tuch is the reminder of what happens when too much of that opportunity slips away. At $4.75 million annually, he gave Buffalo a productive top-line winger at a price that should have made building around him easier. He scored at least 33 goals in three of his final four seasons with the Sabres. That was exactly the kind of contract teams need when they are trying to assemble a contender, and Buffalo spent most of its portion of that deal outside the playoffs.



The 2026 breakthrough deserves credit. Buffalo finally returned to the postseason and beat Boston for its first playoff series victory since 2007. That mattered to the players and to a fan base that had waited far too long. But one successful spring at the end of Tuch’s bargain contract does not erase the opportunity lost before it. Imagine what several years of meaningful games and playoff experience could have done for this core.



There is also a difference between criticizing how Buffalo used Tuch’s affordable years and believing the team should have paid whatever it took to keep him. His move to Washington came with an eight-year, $84 million contract. Passing on that commitment is defensible, while still acknowledging that Buffalo should have done more when he cost a fraction of that price. The mistake was allowing so much of the bargain to expire before the team became competitive.



This lesson needs to guide the next decisions. Prospects and draft picks have value, including their ability to bring in established players who help Thompson and Dahlin now. Buffalo should keep developing young talent, but it also needs to recognize when waiting for another player to become ready costs more than making a trade. With every significant move, the question should be whether it improves the team’s chances during this window. The Hellebuyck drama will be monitored closely, but he will be a difference-maker wherever he goes. With Ruff liking Thompson on the wing, the team’s two biggest holes are a legit #1 center and a goalie, both of whom can steal games on their own. Their depth is what made the Sabres great last year, and the current roster should be the same.



The Sabres do not automatically stop being contenders when Thompson’s contract expires. Players can re-sign, younger teammates can take on larger roles, and a good organization can extend its success. But Buffalo cannot assume the same combination of production, cost, and health will still be available years from now. They already let most of Tuch’s bargain deal pass without taking advantage. Thompson and Dahlin should not reach the end of theirs with Buffalo still explaining how promising the future looks. Both are playing their best hockey and still have many prime years left.



Benson, Doan, and Ostlund are all locked up now on long-term deals at $7 million cap hit or less. The Sabres currently have just over $29 million in cap space for next year with 15 players signed. Their UFAs are Zucker, Danforth, Carrick, Timmins, Lyon, and Ellis (unless he plays 12 games, he will remain an RFA). Their RFAs on the roster are Quinn (arb. rights), Kulich, and Crevier. Between Lyon and Ellis, one of them will definitely be re-signed, with Ellis ahead in that race. Zucker could be re-signed at a reduced rate, while the others will likely walk. With the three RFAs, they’ll need a great season to land a big-money, long-term contract. So there is plenty of room to add real difference-makers this season and next summer.



Go for it, Jarmo; the whole city is behind you now. Just making the playoffs isn’t good enough, and I think he knows that.

stories.title: Buffalo Sabres Top 25 Under 25: #2: Owen Power
stories.summary:
The Top 25 Under 25 is a collaboration by members of the Die By The Blade community. 92 readers ranked Buffalo Sabres players under the age of 25 as of August 1, 2026. Each participant used their own metric of current ability and production to rank each player.



Owen Power



Drafted: 2021 – 1st Round (1st Overall)



Position: Defense



Born: November 22nd, 2002 – 23 Years Old



2025-2026 Stats: GP 81 G 8 A 21 PTS 29 / Playoffs GP 13 G 0 A 6 PTS 6, NHL



2025 T25U25 Ranking: 1



Owen Power continues to be a core piece of the Sabres roster. He’s been in the top 5 in these rankings since being drafted in 2021. Despite the carousel of defensive partners, Power has taken significant strides in his game.



Last season, he saw a dip in his offensive production, but his defensive effectiveness was noticeably improved. He took on more of a “stay-at-home” role to allow Bowen Byram to operate more freely. His impact was noticeable and can been seen on his stat line as his plus minus went from a -13 in 2024-25 to +9 this past year. He was also heavily utilized on the penalty kill. Out of the Sabres big 4 of Power-Byram-Dahlin-Samuelsson, Power was second in shorthanded time on ice with just over 150 minutes shorthanded. This was a career high and a 30% increase in time from the prior year. The Sabres had the 4th best penalty kill last season due in no small part to Power’s defensive progression.



Even though his defense was the most noticeable improvement in his game, Power still provides significant offensive production from the back end. His skating makes him a threat to create offense on each shift. When he gets going on the rush, he can be hard to stop.




Owen Power attempts to go coast to coast but Korpisalo stops him #LetsGoBuffalo #NHLBruins pic.twitter.com/dlKfLAevBc— Buffalo Hockey Moments (@SabresPlays) December 28, 2025




He’s at his best offensively when he’s joining the rush or playing with a rover mindset in the offensive zone. His ability to get pucks through traffic has improved over the years:




OWEN POWER SENDS IT HOME! #LetsGoBuffalo pic.twitter.com/rdsWxwF2Su— Buffalo Sabres (@BuffaloSabres) February 1, 2026




His playoff performance, particularly against Montreal, was excellent. He was the most consistent defender against Boston. He took his game up a notch against Montreal. Even after suffering a significant injury in game 5, he was one of the Sabres best players in that series.



With the exit of Byram, he’ll once again be looking for a new defensive partner, but he’s shown to be effective regardless of who he’s lining up with. The versatility in his game allows him to be impactful regardless of the situation. He may not always pop off the screen, but if you look closely at his game, the countless little plays he makes add up to an invaluable impact on the Buffalo Sabres.

stories.title: Buffalo Sabres Top 25 Under 25: #3 Josh Doan
stories.summary:
The Top 25 Under 25 is a collaboration by members of the Die By The Blade community. 92 readers ranked Buffalo Sabres players under the age of 25 as of August 1, 2026. Each participant used their own metric of current ability and production to rank each player.



Josh Doan



Drafted: 2021 Second Round, #37 overall



Size: 6’2″, 198 lbs



Position: Winger (shoots right)



Born: 2/1/2002 (Age: 24) Scottsdale, AZ



2025-2026 stats: GP82 G25 A27 PTS52, Buffalo Sabres (NHL)



2025 T25U25 Ranking: 8th



This is how we started last year’s T25U25 for Doan – 




It’s truly unfortunate that every movement Josh Doan makes is going to be examined under the microscope of the JJ Peterka trade. In case you forgot, the 23-year-old comes to Buffalo along with defenseman Michael Kesselring from Utah Mammoth with the young German forward going the other way. It definitely was a controversial trade that many will say the Sabres got fleeced in, while others maintain that as long as both sides get what they wanted out of it, it’s a fair hockey trade. Only time will tell.




A year later, Kesselring is a distant memory traded away to the Sharks for the Sabres to move up seven spots in the Draft and pick up Ilia Morozov. Meanwhile Doan has been an unqualified success, logging 52 points outscoring Peterka who had 47 points and was then flipped to the Boston Bruins for two first rounders, in 2026 and 2028. 



The Son of Doan has become an integral part of the Sabres top six, getting minutes on the right side of the powerplay unit as well. His 17 points with the man advantage was third behind only Rasmus Dahlin and Tage Thompson.









So where does Josh Doan go from here? 



Buffalo tried real hard to keep Alex Tuch, and reports indicate they were willing to pay him nearly $10 million a year too, but eventually the Syracuse-native decided he wanted to go to Washington instead. At some point the Sabres decided that Doan was an in-house, more than ready-made replacement for him, especially since the 24-year-old led Buffalo with 2.12 takeaways per 60, while Tuch was at 1.55. 



Doan is not afraid to be physical, throwing the body where needed with 3.59 hits/60, but it’s the timing of when he chooses to do so was what was incredible, especially in the Bruins series when it went up to 7.07 hits/60.









Doan signed a seven-year, $48.65 million contract extension in January 2026, which is actually just higher in AAV than the extension Noah Ostlund signed yesterday. For the $6.95 million AAV, the Sabres are certainly getting excellent value for what they have him locked up for, with comparables such as Troy Terry who matched his scoring output in just 51 games, Nazem Kadri who had 50 pts in 77 GP and Anders Lee who got to 42 pts in 82 GP.



He’s quickly become a fan favorite with his work ethic and Doan has shown that he is indeed his father’s son with his no prisoners taken playing style. The Sabres certainly got a gem of a hockey player in Josh Doan.

stories.title: Buffalo Sabres sign Noah Ostlund to long-term extension
stories.summary:
With training camp just around the corner, the Buffalo Sabres announced that young forward Noah Ostlund has inked an eight-year extension with an AAV of $6.6 million. This represents a handsome raise for the 22-year-old who has seen his role with the Sabres grow in the last couple of seasons, with Ostlund entering the last year of his current three-year deal an AAV of just $886,666. 



Ostlund played in eight games in Buffalo in the 2024-25 season but became indispensable with the Rochester Americans, going 45GP 19G 17A 36pts. However, last season he made the step up and scored 3G and 7A in ten games for the Amerks, but spent the majority of the time with the Sabres playing in 60 games, with 11G and 16A for 27 points in all. It was in the playoffs though that he made the biggest impression, and irreversibly turned the series against the Boston Bruins in the Sabres favor in just three games before he went out injured. Buffalo could have certainly used him in the tight series to come with the Montreal Canadiens when they were edged out in overtime of Game 7. 



The Swedish-born forward is expected to stay in Buffalo this season and compete for a spot in the top six, and extending him at a cost-controlled rate represents excellent value again for the Sabres who have built up a stable of young talent all at reasonable cap hits. 



It does appear that the Sabres’ comparable for the extension they handed Ostlund was Frank Nazar of the Chicago Blackhawks, who was given a 7-year extension last summer for $6.60M AAV, and he potted 15 goals and 26 assists for 41 points in 66 games last season. 



What is fascinating about this contract is that it’s more in the line of the “Dylan Cozens / Tage Thompson” style max-term roll of the dice—buying up almost entirely UFA years based on projection rather than the traditional 2-to-3-year bridge deals at a lower dollar amount. Clearly Ostlund also believes in whatever Jarmo Kekäläinen is selling because he is choosing to commit his long-term future to Buffalo.
